In the middle of the Danube river separating Serbia and Romania, a rusty hull is visible along with a broken mast. The ship, near the Serbian port of Prahovo, laden with weapons, belonged to Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet. Baking temperatures and drought have driven water levels to record lows across large parts of central and eastern Europe, exposing historic and prehistoric relics. Extreme conditions aggravated by the climate emergency have left Europe's waterways from the Netherlands to the Black Sea parched. The ground is dry where cruise ships and ferries once docked. Fishermen are out of work, vessels are stranded and crucial power plants are on the brink of closure. Flows through the Danube, Europe's second-longest river, are the lowest they've been in decades, exposing rocks, old shipwrecks, a WWII bomb and even the remains of an extinct species. At least 20 World War II wrecks are visible to the naked eye from the banks of Prahovo. Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in September 1944 near Prahovo in the Danube gorge as they came under Soviet fire. The idea behind the deliberate sinking was to slow down the Soviet advance in the Balkans. But Nazi Germany surrendered months later, in May 1945. Over in the Bulgarian village of Ryahovo, residents discovered the bones of what is believed to be a woolly mammoth. Rousse Regional Museum of History director Nikolay Nenov said scientists had so far identified a jawbone, fragments of tusks, part of a shoulder blade and a femur. In the port city of Vidin, almost 200 tourists had to be evacuated from a cruise ship after it ran into a shoal. Meanwhile, authorities in Budapest were forced to close the Margaret Bridge after a wartime bomb was exposed at its base. Experts have linked the record low water levels to global warming and other factors. According to the Copernicus climate service, Europe is the fastest-warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average. It is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires. In Serbia, hundreds of small boats and dozens of cargo ships are marooned on the dried-out river bank near the northern city of Novi Sad. Houseboat owner Radovan Segrt, who runs river excursions on his vessel, told The Associated Press that the water in the Danube had withdrawn "some 15 to 20 meters from its shore". "The summer season is over now, as far as boat riding is concerned," he said. At the Vidin-Calafat Bridge connecting Bulgaria and Romania, Bulgarians said they were out of work because the low water levels had trapped their boats onshore. "It's never dried up this much before," fisherman Rossen Dobrev told Agence France-Presse. "Now we can even walk all the way to Romania." But it is not just Serbia, Bulgaria and Romania that are suffering. In Germany and the Netherlands, water levels on the Rhine also fell to record lows, triggered by heatwaves and prolonged dry weather. Shallow Rhine waters have forced reductions of cargo on ‌vessels to about 20 per cent of their normal capacity, sparking concerns about the economic fallout of having to limit navigation and shipping. The Rhine is a crucial shipping artery for grains, minerals, ore, coal and oil products. Marcel Beck, manager of the western German ports of Neuss, Düsseldorf and Cologne at RheinCargo, said the water levels were having a "devastating impact" on shipping. "A ship that would normally carry 2,000 to 2,500 metric tons of cargo can now only transport 400, perhaps 600, metric tons depending on the ship's design," he said. "This places an enormous burden on the entire transport chain to reorganise everything in order to still get the goods inland." Meanwhile, in the United Kingdom, half of England and the whole of Wales are officially in drought. July is set to be the driest month on record as extreme heat continues. The dry spell has also led to shrinking rivers and lakes. The Environment Agency said nearly 80 per cent of England's rivers were seeing flows below normal or lower. The River Thames at Reading has recorded its lowest level on record. Firefighters responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record. For the first time in their history, Hungary and Romania had to shut down atomic reactors normally cooled by the Danube. The largest nuclear power plant in Hungary, the 44-year-old Paks, had been producing at one point only 240 megawatts of power rather than the usual 2,000. Hungarian authorities have asked citizens to reduce energy use in the peak evening hours. In Romania, the Danube's water flow fell to 1,500 cubic metres per second, less than a third of its July average, according to the National Institute of Hydrology. Authorities have already shut down one reactor unit at the Cernavoda plant for safety reasons, which provides about 20 per cent of the country's power. Acting Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan also appealed to citizens to voluntarily limit electricity usage in peak evening hours. Romanian authorities even needed to conduct a controlled explosion in the river to direct cooling water to its sole operational nuclear plant. Two car plants in Romania run by Dacia and Ford have agreed to halt production for more than a fortnight to reduce electricity consumption. In Serbia, record-low Danube levels have pushed the country's key hydro-electric plant to operate with only 20 per cent of its capacity. Water levels are not expected to rise on the Danube in the coming days or even weeks as no significant rainfall is forecast. ABC with wires

https://www.dw.com/en/new-fighting-in-et.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5N9nB Alula Aba Nega International Airport in Tigray: flights have been supendended Image: Liu Fangqiang/Xinhua/picture alliance Advertisement The fighting reported in and around Ethiopia's northern Tigray region marks more than another episode of tension between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the region's leadership. It raises a fundamental question: What remains of the fragile peace established in 2022 — and where does the conflict go from here? From 2020 to 2022, Ethiopia was devastated by a civil war between the federal government in Addis Ababa and Tigray's regional leadership. The conflict drew in neighboring regions and foreign troops from Eritrea, leading to a humanitarian crisis that displaced millions and left hundreds of thousands dead. While a peace agreement halted the worst of the bloodshed in late 2022, it left a lot of the political and territorial disputes unresolved. DW spoke to witnesses in the towns of Abala and Erebti on the border with Tigray who confirmed that new fighting had taken place there between Tigray forces and Ethiopian federal troops. Humanitarian sources also reported clashes in the area. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, citing the "current situation in the Tigray region." Reports that Tigray forces have taken control of airports in the region could not independently be verified by DW. For Oslo-based peace researcher Kjetil Tronvoll, however, the latest developments represent a decisive escalation. "I think the war has already begun," Tronvoll told DW. German security analyst Gerrit Kurtz of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin also sees the developments as a serious escalation. "This is a step towards a war," he told DW. Two competing narratives The two sides are presenting fundamentally different accounts of what triggered the latest escalation . In a statement issued on September 23, the National Regional Government of Tigray said its forces had been responding defensively to an attack by the federal government . It accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of launching a new "genocidal invasion" and said Tigray forces had been ordered to defend the population. The Tigray government also accused Addis Ababa of carrying out air and drone strikes and artillery attacks in recent months. It said it had previously refrained from responding to what it described as repeated provocations in an effort to de-escalate the situation. The allegations could not independently be verified. The federal government, meanwhile, has portrayed the developments as part of a broader coordinated threat involving armed groups opposed to the prime minister. The competing narratives illustrate one of the central problems facing any renewed peace effort: The parties do not even agree on the basic interpretation of the escalation. A fragile peace under pressure The current crisis cannot be separated from the shortcomings of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. The deal ended two years of devastating war between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), but it did not resolve some of the conflict's underlying political and territorial disputes. Western Tigray remains particularly contentious. The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people remains unresolved, while questions over Tigray's political representation and its relationship with the federal government continue to fuel tensions. "The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting, but it did not resolve the underlying political conflict," Tronvoll says. At the heart of that conflict is a fundamental disagreement over Ethiopia's political order. The TPLF has traditionally defended a strong federal structure and substantial regional autonomy. Abiy Ahmed's government has pursued a more centralized political model. The issue is therefore not simply whether individual provisions of the peace agreement are implemented. It is also about competing visions of how Ethiopia should be governed. Former enemies join forces The emergence of an alliance of seven armed groups opposing Abiy adds another layer of complexity. The grouping includes the TPLF, Fano forces from the state of Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army from another regional state within Ethiopia. Some of these organizations were bitter enemies during the Tigray war. Their decision to cooperate therefore represents a significant political development — but not necessarily a durable alliance. Kurtz says the alliance has been developing for some time and that some of its leaders have apparently already met. "It was a very important development," he says. "The alliance has been in the making for a long time." At the same time, he points to the fundamental differences between its members. "All the political differences that they have are certainly there to resolve once their overall joint aim is achieved, which is overthrowing the government of Abiy." Tronvoll similarly describes the cooperation as primarily tactical. The question is whether the groups can turn their shared opposition to Abiy into a lasting political and military strategy. There is another complicating factor: Eritrea. The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of supporting the alliance. Eritrea has rejected such allegations. Kurtz says there have been reports of contacts between the armed groups and Eritrea, but stresses that the new alliance itself appears to be a domestic grouping. The geography of the alliance is another obstacle. Its members operate in different parts of Ethiopia and pursue different political objectives. Coordinating military operations across such distances would be difficult. Ethiopian security forces in 2021 after they took control of Amhara city from the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) Image: Minasse Wondimu Hailu/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance Can the escalation still be contained? The most urgent question is whether the current fighting can still be contained before it develops into another full-scale war. Kurtz argues that the immediate priority is straightforward: The forces involved in the fighting need to stop. "Both the Ethiopian armed forces as well as the Tigray security forces are involved in active hostilities right now. So they should stop this," he says. But bringing the fighting to an end will require more than a ceasefire on the ground. Ethiopia's conflict has become increasingly fragmented. Armed groups are operating not only in Tigray, but also in Amhara and Oromia, two other regional states within Ethiopia. Regional actors such as Eritrea are potentially also playing a role. The new crisis facing Tigray’s families To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Who can mediate? International actors have repeatedly warned about the risk of renewed conflict. Yet sustained diplomatic engagement has so far failed to produce a new political process. The United States remains an important actor, according to Kurtz, but he says Washington has not shown sufficient engagement. The African Union, the European Union and other international actors could also play a role. The challenge is that there is no single actor with enough influence over all the parties. "It will require a certain coalition of efforts," Kurtz says. He argues that preventing a wider war would require a broader diplomatic push, with international actors dividing responsibilities and coordinating their efforts. The United Nations General Assembly in New York could provide an opportunity for international leaders to engage directly with the Ethiopian government, he says. But diplomacy would also have to address the armed groups involved in the new alliance. Tronvoll is similarly critical of the international response so far. He argues that the warning signs had been visible for some time but that international efforts to bring the parties back to negotiations remained limited. The political problem remains For the people of Tigray, the stakes are particularly high. The region has yet to recover from the consequences of the 2020-2022 war. Many people remain displaced, infrastructure has been severely damaged and the economic recovery remains fragile. A return to large-scale war would therefore not simply mean a resumption of an old conflict. It could open a new and potentially broader phase of Ethiopia's wider security crisis, particularly given the simultaneous conflicts in Amhara and Oromia. The immediate priority is to prevent the latest fighting from developing into a wider war. But any sustainable settlement will have to address the political questions that the 2022 agreement left unresolved. The key question is therefore not simply whether the war has returned. It is whether Ethiopia and its international partners can still create enough diplomatic space to prevent the latest escalation from closing the door to a political solution.
